Solution:
Let G be a cubic Hamiltonian graph. Prove that the number of distinct Hamilton
cycles contained in G is at least 3.
To prove that a cubic Hamiltonian graph contains at least three distinct Hamilton cycles,
we rely on a fundamental result in graph theory known as Smith’s Theorem. We will first
state and prove Smith’s Theorem, and then use it to derive the existence of at least three
Hamilton cycles.
Definitions and Preliminaries
Let G = (V, E) be a simple, cubic (3-regular) graph that is Hamiltonian. A Hamilton
cycle is a cycle that visits every vertex of G exactly once. We denote the set of all Hamilton
cycles in G by H. Since G is Hamiltonian, |H| ≥1.
Part 1: Smith’s Theorem
Theorem (Smith, 1946): In any cubic graph, the number of Hamilton cycles containing
any fixed edge e is even.
Proof: Let G be a cubic graph with n vertices. Fix an edge e = {u, v} ∈E. We consider
the set P of all Hamilton paths in G that start with the vertex u followed by the vertex v.
That is, a path P ∈P is a sequence of vertices v1, v2, . . . , vn such that v1 = u, v2 = v, and
{vi, vi+1} ∈E for all 1 ≤i < n.
We construct an auxiliary ”exchange graph” Γ whose vertices are the paths in P. We
define the edges of Γ based on a path transformation operation known as *rotation*.
Let P = u, v, . . . , w be a path in P, where w = vn is the endpoint. Since G is cubic,
the vertex w has exactly three neighbors in G. One of these neighbors is vn−1 (the vertex
preceding w on P). Let the other two neighbors be x and y. 1. Case 1: Cycle formation.
If one of the neighbors, say x, is the starting vertex u, then the path P can be extended
to a Hamilton cycle C = P ∪{w, u} containing the edge e. 2. Case 2: Rotation. If a
neighbor z ∈{x, y} is not u, then z must be some internal vertex vi of the path P (where
2 < i < n −1). The edge {w, vi} forms a cycle within the path structure. We can form a
new Hamilton path P ′ starting with u, v by adding the edge {w, vi} and removing the edge
{vi, vi+1}. The new path traverses u . . . vi, then jumps to w, and traverses backwards to vi+1.
This operation connects P to P ′ in Γ.
Analysis of Degrees in Γ: For any path P ∈P ending at w: * The vertex w has 3
incident edges in G. One is part of P. * This leaves 2 edges connecting w to other vertices.
Let these neighbors be z1, z2. * Since G is simple, at most one of z1, z2 can be u (since u is
already connected to v). * If neither z1 nor z2 is u, then both provide valid rotations. Thus,
P has degree 2 in Γ. * If one neighbor (say z1) is u, then P corresponds to a Hamilton cycle.
The other neighbor (z2) provides exactly one rotation. Thus, P has degree 1 in Γ.
The graph Γ consists of disjoint paths and cycles. The vertices of Γ with degree 1 are
the endpoints of the path components in Γ. By the Handshaking Lemma, the number of
vertices with odd degree in any graph must be even. Therefore, the number of paths in P
that can be extended to a Hamilton cycle is even.
Since there is a one-to-one correspondence between paths in P that extend to a cycle
(by adding the edge {w, u}) and Hamilton cycles containing e (by removing the edge {w, u}
adjacent to u but not v), the number of Hamilton cycles containing e is even.
Part 2: Existence of at least 3 Hamilton Cycles
We now use Smith’s Theorem to prove that |H| ≥3.
1. First Cycle: Since G is Hamiltonian, there exists at least one Hamilton cycle, which
we call H1.
2. Second Cycle: Choose any edge e1 ∈E(H1). By Smith’s Theorem, the number of
Hamilton cycles containing e1 is even. Since H1 contains e1, there must be at least one other
Hamilton cycle H2 such that e1 ∈E(H2) and H2 ̸= H1.
3. Third Cycle: Since H1 and H2 are distinct Hamilton cycles, their edge sets are
not identical. Thus, the set difference E(H2) \ E(H1) is non-empty. Let e2 be an edge in
Apply Smith’s Theorem to the edge e2. The number of Hamilton cycles containing e2
must be even. We know that: * H2 contains e2. * H1 does not contain e2.
Since the count must be even and at least one cycle (H2) contains e2, there must exist
another Hamilton cycle H3 such that e2 ∈E(H3) and H3 ̸= H2.
4. Distinctness: We have identified three cycles H1, H2, H3. * H1 ̸= H2 by construction
(step 2). * H2 ̸= H3 by construction (step 3). * To check if H3 ̸= H1, observe that e2 ∈E(H3)
but e2 /∈E(H1) (since e2 was chosen from E(H2) \ E(H1)). Therefore, H3 ̸= H1.
Thus, H1, H2, and H3 are three distinct Hamilton cycles in G.
Conclusion: Every cubic Hamiltonian graph contains at least 3 distinct Hamilton cycles.
